title: KINDER: Kernel-based Independence for Fair Representation Learning via Prototype-space Erasure
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Prior erasure finds its subspace indirectly through adversaries; ours builds it directly from group prototypes and lowers dependence measures.
layout: 4 panels: two stacked pipelines left, two bar charts right; dashed borders
description: The left side stacks two nearly identical pipeline diagrams. Panel (a), in a gray dashed border, shows prior projection-based concept erasure. Input goes to a frozen Encoder, then a "dirty" representation, a teal Projection-Based Concept Erasure block, a "clean" representation, a Head and Loss. A red backpropagate arrow points back at the Head. An expanded teal strip underneath shows Probe/Adversary, Subspace and Projection, with "subspace identified indirectly". Panel (b), in a purple border, has the same flow with a purple KINDER Block. Its expanded strip shows Lifting to Kernel Space, Group Prototypes, Subspace identified through prototypes, and Projection. The backpropagate arrow reaches the Encoder. Two gold-bordered bar charts on the right, (c) RBF-HSIC and (d) Average Gap, compare BERT, SUP, INLP, RLACE, KCE and KINDER. KINDER is highlighted in gold or pink and is lowest in both.
caption: Overview of prior projection-based concept erasure and KINDER. (a) Prior methods identify an erasable subspace indirectly through decoder-specific objectives. (b) KINDER instead builds protected-group prototypes in a lifted feature space and removes the directions along which those group prototypes differ. (c–d) After applying KINDER on Moji, the representation should contain less protected-group information and smaller group-level distribution differences. This is shown by lower HSIC and average gap values. Significance tests are reported in Appendix E.2.
abstract: Concept erasure is a prominent approach to achieving fairness in machine learning through the removal of sensitive attributes from learned representations. Prior concept erasure methods typically define debiasing indirectly through the failure of a chosen adversary, probe, or fairness penalty, which makes the target of erasure dependent on a particular decoder family or optimization setup. We introduce KINDER, which directly removes sensitive-attribute information from intermediate representations with respect to a chosen family of prototype functionals, and is compatible with any deep model containing an intermediate feature space, independent of the architecture, task type, or training paradigm. KINDER operates in a random Fourier feature space, where it estimates a sensitive subspace from protected group prototypes and projects representations onto its orthogonal complement. Thus, it forms an explicit representation cleaning mechanism distinct from prior fairness control studies. We conduct extensive experiments across diverse settings and show the effectiveness of KINDER on (i) supervised and self-supervised settings, (ii) classification, regression, and image segmentation tasks, and (iii) diverse data modalities, including visual, textual, and tabular data. Code and trained models are available at: https://github.com/abtinmU/KINDER
